title: OAuth for MCP, step by step
heading: How an agent gets access and refresh tokens
lead: An agent such as Claude Code wants to use a remote MCP server that holds your data. The server will not serve a stranger, and you should never type your password into the agent. OAuth solves this with four roles and one short dance: the agent discovers who issues tokens for the server, sends **you** to a browser to sign in and approve, receives a one-time code, and trades that code for two tokens. The **access token** goes on every request and dies within an hour. The **refresh token** lives longer and quietly buys new access tokens. Eight numbered topics follow every message in order and show exactly what each one carries.

facts.text: you: the person whose data it is and who says yes or no
the agent (here Claude Code); it asks for access and holds the tokens, never your password
the MCP server; it checks the access token on every request and serves tools and data
signs you in, asks for your consent and mints the tokens; run by the server's owner or an identity provider
a short-lived bearer credential sent as `Authorization: Bearer …` on every request to one server
a long-lived secret the agent exchanges for a fresh access token when the old one expires, without bothering you

versions.label: Mar '25
versions.note: Authorization enters the spec: OAuth 2.1 with PKCE, metadata discovery and dynamic client registration. The MCP server is both resource and authorization server.

versions.label: Jun '25
versions.note: The MCP server becomes a plain resource server: its metadata points at the authorization server, and tokens are bound to one server with the resource parameter.

versions.label: Nov '25
versions.note: Client ID metadata documents join dynamic registration, and a server can ask for more scope step by step.

topics.title: 1 · Connect and get challenged
topics.subtitle: The first request has no token and is refused

body: Nothing in OAuth starts with a login screen. It starts with the client simply trying. Claude sends the first MCP request, `initialize`, with no credentials at all. A server that requires authorization answers **401 Unauthorized** and adds a `WWW-Authenticate` header: the HTTP way of saying "you need a bearer token, and here is where to learn how to get one".

What is passed matters. The request carries the MCP protocol version and the client's name. The 401 carries one URL, `resource_metadata`, pointing at a small JSON document the server publishes about itself. That single pointer is what makes the rest automatic: no server URL to configure, no list of identity providers built into the agent.

items: The 401 carries `resource_metadata`, a URL to the protected resource metadata document (RFC 9728).
Before this revision the 401 was bare and the client assumed the MCP server issued its own tokens.

steps.title: You add the server
steps.explanation: You tell Claude about a remote MCP server by its URL. Nothing else: no username, no password, no key. Claude will work out how to get in by asking the server itself.

messages.name: add server https://mcp.example.com/mcp
messages.info: carries: the server URL only

steps.title: Claude knocks without a token
steps.explanation: Claude sends the first MCP request, initialize, to the server's endpoint. It carries the protocol version Claude speaks and Claude's name and version. There is no Authorization header yet, on purpose: the server's answer will tell Claude what it needs.

messages.name: POST /mcp · initialize
messages.info: carries: protocolVersion, clientInfo; no Authorization header

annotations.text: No `Authorization` header. The client has nothing to send yet.
`initialize` is always the first MCP request. The server never runs it here; it stops at the missing token.
The spec revision the client speaks. The server will answer with the one it accepts.

steps.title: The server answers 401 and points to its metadata
steps.explanation: The MCP server refuses. Its 401 carries a WWW-Authenticate header with the scheme Bearer, which means "send me a bearer token", and a resource_metadata URL, which is where Claude goes next to learn who issues tokens for this server.

messages.name: 401 Unauthorized
messages.info: carries: WWW-Authenticate: Bearer resource_metadata=<URL>

annotations.text: The scheme `Bearer` tells the client which kind of credential to present: a token in the Authorization header.
The URL of the protected resource metadata (RFC 9728). Claude fetches it in the next topic.

messages.name: 401 Unauthorized
messages.info: carries: WWW-Authenticate: Bearer, nothing else

annotations.text: In the first revision there was no pointer. The client assumed the MCP server was also the authorization server.

topics.title: 2 · Discover where to sign in
topics.subtitle: Two metadata documents name every endpoint

body: OAuth servers describe themselves in JSON documents at well-known URLs, so a client never needs them configured. There are two. The **protected resource metadata** belongs to the MCP server and says: this is my identifier, these are the authorization servers that protect me, these are the scopes I understand. The **authorization server metadata** (RFC 8414) belongs to the authorization server and lists its endpoints: where to send the browser (`authorization_endpoint`), where to exchange codes for tokens (`token_endpoint`), where a client may register, and which code challenge methods it accepts.
Claude reads both, checks that the authorization server supports PKCE with `S256`, and now knows every URL it will need for the rest of the flow.

steps.title: Read the protected resource metadata
steps.explanation: Claude fetches the URL from the 401. The MCP server answers with its own identifier, the list of authorization servers that protect it and the scopes it understands. Claude now knows which authorization server to talk to.

messages.name: GET /.well-known/oauth-protected-resource
messages.info: carries: nothing; a plain GET

messages.name: 200 OK · resource metadata
messages.info: carries: resource, authorization_servers, scopes_supported

annotations.text: The server's identifier. Claude will ask for tokens bound to exactly this value, so a token for this server works nowhere else.
Who issues tokens for this server. Claude picks one and fetches its metadata next.
The permissions the server understands; Claude requests a subset at sign-in.
`header` only: the token goes in the Authorization header, never in a URL.

2025-03-26.title: Assume the server issues its own tokens
2025-03-26.explanation: The first revision had no protected resource metadata. Claude took the MCP server's own origin as the authorization server and looked for the authorization server metadata there.

messages.name: authorization server = https://mcp.example.com
messages.info: derived from the MCP endpoint's origin

steps.title: Fetch the authorization server metadata
steps.explanation: Claude asks the authorization server for its well-known metadata. The answer carries the issuer name and the three endpoints the flow needs: authorize, token and register, plus the PKCE methods and the grant types it supports.

messages.name: GET /.well-known/oauth-authorization-server
messages.info: carries: nothing; a plain GET

messages.name: 200 OK · server metadata
messages.info: carries: issuer, authorization/token/registration endpoints, S256, grant types

annotations.text: The server's identity. Claude stores tokens keyed by it, so two servers behind different issuers never mix.
Where the browser is sent in topic 4.
Where the code is exchanged for tokens in topic 5, and where refresh happens in topic 7.
Must include `S256`. Claude refuses to continue without PKCE.
`authorization_code` for the sign-in, `refresh_token` for silent renewal.
`none` lets a public client like Claude, which cannot keep a secret, use PKCE alone.

steps.title: Check PKCE support
steps.explanation: Before anything leaves the machine, Claude checks the metadata: the code grant must be supported and S256 must be listed. If either is missing, the server cannot be used safely and Claude stops here.

messages.name: verify metadata
messages.info: code grant and S256 present; endpoints noted
messages.payload:
response_types_supported     includes "code"        ok
code_challenge_methods       includes "S256"        ok
authorization_endpoint       https://auth.example.com/authorize
token_endpoint               https://auth.example.com/token
registration_endpoint        https://auth.example.com/register   (optional)

body: Every OAuth client has a `client_id`, a public name the authorization server knows it by. Web apps get one when a developer registers them by hand. An agent connects to servers nobody registered it with, so MCP needs a way to introduce a client on the fly. **Dynamic client registration** (RFC 7591) does this: Claude posts a short description of itself, including the loopback address it will listen on, and receives a `client_id` in return. Public clients like Claude get no secret, because a program on a laptop cannot keep one.

The November 2025 revision added a second way, **client ID metadata documents**: the `client_id` is itself an `https` URL under the client publisher's control, and the authorization server fetches the client's description from there. No registration call, and the server can see who publishes the client.

items: Client ID metadata documents: the `client_id` is an `https` URL the authorization server dereferences for the client's metadata.

steps.title: Register dynamically
steps.explanation: Claude posts its description to the registration endpoint: a display name, the loopback redirect URI where the browser should come back, the grant types it will use, and token_endpoint_auth_method none. The server answers with the client_id Claude will use from now on.

messages.name: POST /register
messages.info: carries: client_name, redirect_uris, grant_types, auth method none

annotations.text: A loopback address on your machine. The browser will be sent back here with the code; only a program on this machine can receive it.
Claude declares both grants it will use: the code exchange now and refresh later.
`none`: no client secret. PKCE will prove that the code exchange comes from the same program that started the sign-in.

messages.name: 201 Created · client_id
messages.info: carries: client_id, the registered redirect URIs

annotations.text: Public, not secret. Meaningful only to this authorization server; Claude stores it next to the tokens.

steps.title: Or present a client ID metadata document
steps.explanation: Instead of registering, Claude can use an https URL as its client_id. The authorization server fetches the document behind that URL, reads the client's name and redirect URIs from it, and trusts the publisher of the domain to describe their own client.

messages.name: client_id = https://client.example/.well-known/oauth-client
messages.info: an https URL under the publisher's control

messages.name: GET the client_id URL
messages.info: carries back: client_name, redirect_uris, auth method

annotations.text: Must equal the URL the document was fetched from.
The server redirects only to URIs listed here, so a document published by the real client publisher protects its users.

2025-03-26.title: Not yet specified
2025-03-26.explanation: Client ID metadata documents arrive in the 2025-11-25 revision. In this revision a client registers dynamically or has a pre-configured client_id.

2025-06-18.title: Not yet specified
2025-06-18.explanation: Client ID metadata documents arrive in the 2025-11-25 revision. In this revision a client registers dynamically or has a pre-configured client_id.

branches.condition: the client publishes a metadata document

topics.title: 4 · Authorize in the browser
topics.subtitle: You sign in; Claude receives a one-time code

body: This is the only part you see. Claude opens the authorization server's page in your browser. You sign in there, with your password, a passkey or your company's single sign-on, and approve what Claude may do. The authorization server then sends the browser back to a loopback address on your machine with a one-time **authorization code**. Claude never sees your password; it receives only the code.

Two values protect the code. **PKCE**: before opening the browser, Claude generates a random **code verifier** and sends only its hash, the **code challenge**, in the URL. Whoever later redeems the code must present the verifier, which never travelled through the browser. **state**: a random value that comes back with the code so Claude can tell the callback belongs to the request it made. Since the June 2025 revision the request also names the **resource**, the MCP server the token is for.

items: The authorization request carries `resource=` with the MCP server's identifier, so the token is bound to one server.

steps.title: Generate the PKCE pair and a state value
steps.explanation: Claude draws a long random string, the code verifier, and keeps it secret. It hashes it with SHA-256 into the code challenge, which is safe to show in a URL. It also draws a random state value to recognise the callback later.

messages.name: generate code_verifier, code_challenge, state
messages.info: verifier stays on the machine; the challenge is its hash
messages.payload:
code_verifier   = 43–128 random chars from [A-Z a-z 0-9 - . _ ~]   (secret, kept)
code_challenge  = BASE64URL( SHA-256( code_verifier ) )         (goes in the URL)
state           = random string                                 (matches the callback to this request)

steps.title: Open the authorization URL
steps.explanation: Claude starts a tiny web server on a loopback port to catch the callback, then opens the authorization endpoint in your browser. The URL carries: response_type code, Claude's client_id, the loopback redirect URI, the code challenge and its method, the resource (the MCP server), the scopes it wants, and the state.

messages.name: open /authorize?…
messages.info: carries: client_id, redirect_uri, code_challenge, resource, scope, state

annotations.text: `code`: Claude wants an authorization code, not a token, in the browser. The token comes later over the back channel.
Who is asking, from topic 3.
Where the browser must be sent back with the code: a loopback address only a program on your machine can receive.
The hash of the verifier. Seeing it in the browser history gives an attacker nothing.
The MCP server's identifier from topic 2. The token will be minted for that server only.
What Claude asks permission for; you see these on the consent page.
Echoed back by the server so Claude can match the callback to this request.

messages.name: open /authorize?…
messages.info: carries: client_id, redirect_uri, code_challenge, state

annotations.text: Not present in this revision: tokens were not yet bound to one MCP server.

steps.title: You sign in and consent
steps.explanation: The browser loads the authorization server's page. You prove who you are to that server, never to Claude, and the page lists what Claude asked for: the scopes. You approve. The browser posts your consent back to the authorization server.

messages.name: GET /authorize?…
messages.info: carries: the full URL Claude opened

messages.name: 200 · sign-in and consent page
messages.info: carries: the server's own login form and the requested scopes

messages.name: sign in, then approve
messages.info: carries: your password or passkey, to the authorization server only

messages.name: POST /authorize · consent
messages.info: carries: your approval of mcp:tools and mcp:resources

steps.title: The code comes back to Claude
steps.explanation: The authorization server redirects the browser to the loopback address with two values: the one-time authorization code and the state. Claude's tiny server receives them, checks that the state matches, and tells the browser the tab can be closed. The code alone is worthless: redeeming it needs the verifier Claude kept.

messages.name: 302 Found → localhost callback
messages.info: carries: code, state in the Location URL

annotations.text: The authorization code: single use, short-lived, typically under a minute. Useless without the code verifier.
The same value Claude sent. A callback with a different state is ignored.

messages.name: GET /callback?code=…&state=…
messages.info: carries: code, state to Claude's loopback server

messages.name: check state
messages.info: must equal the state from step 1

messages.name: 200 OK · "you can close this tab"
messages.info: carries: a short confirmation page

topics.title: 5 · Exchange the code for tokens
topics.subtitle: Back channel: code + verifier in, access and refresh tokens out

body: Now the browser is out of the picture. Claude talks to the authorization server's token endpoint directly over HTTPS. It sends the code it received, the same redirect URI it used, its client_id, the **code verifier** and the **resource**. The server hashes the verifier, compares it with the challenge it saw when the sign-in started, checks the code is unused and unexpired, and only then answers.

The answer is the goal of the whole flow. The **access token** is a bearer credential: whoever presents it is served, which is why it is scoped, short-lived and bound to one audience. The **refresh token** is a longer-lived secret that lets Claude obtain a new access token later without a browser. Claude stores both in the operating system's credential store, keyed by the authorization server and the MCP server.

steps.title: Send the code and the verifier
steps.explanation: Claude posts to the token endpoint: grant_type authorization_code, the code, the redirect URI used, its client_id, the code verifier and the resource. The verifier is the proof: only the program that generated the challenge can produce it.

messages.name: POST /token
messages.info: carries: grant_type, code, redirect_uri, client_id, code_verifier, resource
messages.payload:
POST /token HTTP/1.1
Host: auth.example.com
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

grant_type=authorization_code
&code=SplxlOBeZQQYbYS6WxSbIA
&redirect_uri=http://localhost:52341/callback
&client_id=cid_8f2a…
&code_verifier=dBjftJeZ4CVP-mB92K27uhbUJU1p1r_wW1gFWFOEjXk
&resource=https://mcp.example.com/mcp

annotations.text: `authorization_code`: exchange a code for tokens.
The one-time code from topic 4.
Must match the one used in the authorization request; a mismatch is refused.
The secret from topic 4, step 1. The server checks BASE64URL(SHA-256(verifier)) equals the stored code_challenge.
Repeated so the issued token is bound to this MCP server.
No client secret: a public client authenticates with PKCE alone.

messages.name: POST /token
messages.info: carries: grant_type, code, redirect_uri, client_id, code_verifier
messages.payload:
POST /token HTTP/1.1
Host: mcp.example.com
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

grant_type=authorization_code
&code=SplxlOBeZQQYbYS6WxSbIA
&redirect_uri=http://localhost:52341/callback
&client_id=cid_8f2a…
&code_verifier=dBjftJeZ4CVP-mB92K27uhbUJU1p1r_wW1gFWFOEjXk

steps.title: Receive the access token and the refresh token
steps.explanation: The authorization server answers with the two tokens. The access token, its type Bearer, its lifetime in seconds, the scope actually granted, and the refresh token. From here on Claude is authorized.

messages.name: 200 OK · tokens
messages.info: carries: access_token, token_type, expires_in, refresh_token, scope

annotations.text: What Claude sends on every request to the MCP server. Opaque to Claude; the server knows how to validate it. Its audience is the MCP server named in `resource`.
`Bearer`: present it as `Authorization: Bearer <token>`.
Seconds until the access token dies, here one hour. Short lifetimes limit the damage of a leak.
Lets Claude get a new access token without a browser. It is the more valuable secret and goes in the keychain.
What was actually granted; it may be less than what was asked.

steps.title: Store both tokens safely
steps.explanation: Claude saves the tokens in the operating system's credential store, keyed by the authorization server's issuer and the MCP server's resource identifier, together with the client_id. Nothing is written to a project file.

messages.name: store credentials
messages.info: OS keychain, keyed by issuer and resource
messages.payload:
keychain entry
  issuer         https://auth.example.com
  resource       https://mcp.example.com/mcp
  client_id      cid_8f2a…
  access_token   at_…        expires 2025-11-25T10:42Z
  refresh_token  rt_…

topics.title: 6 · Use the access token
topics.subtitle: Every MCP request now carries Authorization: Bearer

body: With a token in hand, Claude repeats the very first request, this time with an `Authorization: Bearer` header. The MCP server validates the token: its signature or introspection result, its expiry, its scope, and above all its **audience**, which must be this server. Then the ordinary MCP session begins: initialize, list tools, call tools, each request carrying the same header.
The token is opaque to Claude. It does not read it, parse it or forward it anywhere; it only presents it to the one server it was minted for.

steps.title: Retry the first request with the bearer token
steps.explanation: The same initialize request as in topic 1, now with the header Authorization: Bearer and the access token. Everything else is unchanged.

messages.name: POST /mcp · initialize
messages.info: carries: Authorization: Bearer <access token>, the initialize body
messages.payload:
POST /mcp HTTP/1.1
Host: mcp.example.com
Authorization: Bearer at_2YotnFZFEjr1zCsicMWpAA…
Content-Type: application/json

{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"initialize","params":{"protocolVersion":"2025-11-25","capabilities":{},"clientInfo":{"name":"claude-code","version":"2.x"}}}

annotations.text: The bearer token, in the header only. Never in the URL, never in the JSON body.

steps.title: The server validates the token
steps.explanation: The MCP server checks the token before running anything: the issuer's signature or an introspection call, the expiry time, the scope the request needs, and that the audience is this very server. A token minted for another server is rejected here.

messages.name: validate token
messages.info: signature, expiry, scope, audience = this server
messages.payload:
signature   issuer's key                  ok
expiry      not before now                ok
audience    https://mcp.example.com/mcp   ok   (anything else: reject)
scope       mcp:tools mcp:resources       ok

steps.title: The MCP session proceeds
steps.explanation: The server answers initialize as any MCP server would, and Claude goes on to list and call tools. Every one of those requests carries the same Authorization header until the token expires.

messages.name: 200 OK · initialize result
messages.info: carries: protocolVersion, server capabilities, serverInfo

messages.name: POST /mcp · tools/list
messages.info: carries: Authorization: Bearer, the tools/list request

messages.name: 200 OK · tools
messages.info: carries: the server's tools

fragments.label: the session
fragments.condition: for every request while the access token is valid

topics.title: 7 · Refresh when the access token expires
topics.subtitle: The refresh token buys a new access token, silently

body: Access tokens are deliberately short-lived. When one expires the MCP server answers **401** again, this time with `error="invalid_token"`. Claude does not reopen the browser. It posts the **refresh token** to the token endpoint with `grant_type=refresh_token` and receives a fresh access token, and often a fresh refresh token too. Then it retries the request that failed. You notice nothing.

Many servers rotate refresh tokens: each use returns a new one and invalidates the old. Claude replaces the stored one every time. If the refresh token itself is revoked or expired, the server answers an error and Claude falls back to the full browser sign-in from topic 4.

references.label: OAuth 2.1 draft · refreshing an access token

steps.title: The access token has expired
steps.explanation: An hour later a request fails. The server answers 401 with error invalid_token and a description. This is a different 401 from topic 1: Claude has credentials, they are just stale.

messages.name: POST /mcp · tools/call
messages.info: carries: Authorization: Bearer <expired access token>

messages.name: 401 Unauthorized
messages.info: carries: WWW-Authenticate: Bearer error="invalid_token"
messages.payload:
HTTP/1.1 401 Unauthorized
WWW-Authenticate: Bearer error="invalid_token", error_description="The access token expired"

annotations.text: `invalid_token` means the credential is unusable; `error_description` says why. Claude tries the refresh token before anything else.

steps.title: Send the refresh token
steps.explanation: Claude posts to the token endpoint with grant_type refresh_token, the refresh token, its client_id and the resource. No browser, no user interaction.

messages.name: POST /token
messages.info: carries: grant_type=refresh_token, refresh_token, client_id, resource
messages.payload:
POST /token HTTP/1.1
Host: auth.example.com
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

grant_type=refresh_token
&refresh_token=rt_tGzv3JOkF0XG5Qx2TlKWIA…
&client_id=cid_8f2a…
&resource=https://mcp.example.com/mcp

annotations.text: `refresh_token`: trade a refresh token for a new access token.
The long-lived secret from topic 5. It is sent only here, only to the token endpoint, only over HTTPS.
The new access token must be bound to the same MCP server.

steps.title: New tokens, then retry
steps.explanation: The authorization server answers with a new access token and, when it rotates, a new refresh token. Claude replaces both in the keychain and retries the failed request with the new access token.

messages.name: 200 OK · new tokens
messages.info: carries: access_token, expires_in, and often a new refresh_token

annotations.text: A fresh token for another hour.
A rotated refresh token. The old one stops working; Claude stores the new one.

messages.name: replace stored tokens
messages.info: keychain updated

messages.name: POST /mcp · tools/call
messages.info: carries: Authorization: Bearer <new access token>; the request that failed

messages.name: 200 OK · tool result
messages.info: carries: the tool's result

body: A token carries the scopes you approved. When a tool needs more, a server following the November 2025 revision answers **403 Forbidden** with `error="insufficient_scope"` and the scope it wants. Claude runs the browser sign-in again asking for the union of the old and new scopes, so you approve only the addition and nothing already granted is lost.

items: Scope challenges: a 403 with `insufficient_scope` names the scope a request needs, and the client asks for it incrementally.

steps.title: The server asks for more
steps.explanation: Claude calls a tool that writes. The token only has read scopes, so the server refuses with 403, names the scope it needs and repeats the metadata pointer.

messages.name: POST /mcp · tools/call create_ticket
messages.info: carries: Authorization: Bearer; token has mcp:tools, mcp:resources

messages.name: 403 Forbidden
messages.info: carries: error="insufficient_scope", scope="tickets:write"
messages.payload:
HTTP/1.1 403 Forbidden
WWW-Authenticate: Bearer error="insufficient_scope", scope="tickets:write", resource_metadata="https://mcp.example.com/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource"

annotations.text: What this request needs. Claude asks for the union of what it has and what is missing.

steps.title: Sign in again with the union of scopes
steps.explanation: Claude repeats topic 4 with scope set to the old scopes plus tickets:write, exchanges the code as in topic 5, and retries the tool call with the upgraded token.

messages.name: open /authorize?…&scope=… tickets:write
messages.info: carries: the same parameters as topic 4, with the enlarged scope

messages.name: POST /token
messages.info: carries: the new code and its code_verifier

messages.name: 200 OK · tokens
messages.info: carries: an access token with all three scopes

messages.name: POST /mcp · tools/call create_ticket
messages.info: carries: Authorization: Bearer <upgraded token>

topics.title: Audience binding
topics.subtitle: A token for one server works nowhere else

body: A bearer token is only as safe as the set of places that accept it. If one token worked at every MCP server behind the same authorization server, a rogue server you were tricked into connecting to could replay the token you sent it at the real one. The `resource` parameter in topics 4 and 5 asks for a token whose **audience** is one named server; the authorization server records it in the token; every server rejects tokens whose audience is not itself. This is why the June 2025 revision made `resource` mandatory and why servers must check it.

steps.title: A token minted for one server
steps.explanation: Because Claude named the resource when it asked, the token carries that server as its audience.

messages.name: POST /token
messages.info: carries: resource=https://mcp.example.com/mcp

messages.name: 200 OK · token
messages.info: carries: an access token with aud = mcp.example.com

steps.title: Replayed at another server, and rejected
steps.explanation: Suppose you were tricked into connecting Claude to a rogue server and it received a token minted for itself. It replays that token at the real server. The audience check in topic 6 stops it.

messages.name: POST /mcp
messages.info: carries: a token whose audience is evil.example

messages.name: POST /mcp
messages.info: carries: that same token, replayed

messages.name: validate token
messages.info: aud = evil.example, not this server
messages.payload:
audience   https://evil.example/mcp
expected   https://mcp.example.com/mcp
result     REJECT

messages.name: 401 Unauthorized
messages.info: carries: error="invalid_token"

topics.title: Token passthrough
topics.subtitle: Why the MCP server must not forward Claude's token

body: Many MCP servers wrap another API. The tempting shortcut is to forward the token Claude sent to that upstream API. The spec forbids it: the token's audience is the MCP server, and an upstream that accepts it cannot tell how the request was authorised. A server that forwards tokens becomes a **confused deputy**, lending its authority to whoever reaches it.

The right design is two tokens. Claude's token proves the user to the MCP server. The MCP server obtains its own credentials for the upstream, by token exchange, by its own client credentials, or by a separate consent. Each token means one thing to one audience.

items.text: A token has one audience. If you did not mint or request it for the service you are calling, do not send it there.

steps.title: The tempting shortcut
steps.explanation: The MCP server receives a tool call with Claude's bearer token and simply forwards that token to the upstream API. An upstream that checks audiences rejects it; one that does not has just been fooled.

messages.name: tools/call list_repos
messages.info: carries: Authorization: Bearer at_… (audience: the MCP server)

messages.name: GET /repos
messages.info: carries: Claude's token, forwarded; forbidden
messages.payload:
GET /repos HTTP/1.1
Host: api.example.net
